Title: Binary “Teaching Competencies and Developmental Needs” Assessment (30+ yes/no items)

Purpose and Rationale
This instrument assesses teachers’ educational (developmental) needs by mapping self-reported ability-to-perform or current practice against established domains: planning/preparation, teaching delivery, assessment/feedback, inclusion and special education, collaboration with parents, extracurricular/extended-learning, digital technology usage and knowledge, classroom management/safety, curriculum/subject-matter, and data/information practices. It uses only yes/no responses to reduce response-set and speed administration, while preserving construct fidelity through expert-derived content alignment to professional development frameworks and digital competence taxonomies, and through summative psychometric analysis suitable for binary items. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Professional development needs commonly cluster in instructional development, scientific/subject-area development, personal/organizational development, with sub-dimensions including instructional technologies, material development, assessment/evaluation, and teamwork skills</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Validated needs assessments cover content support, classroom teaching methods, syllabus understanding, lesson planning, assessment/evaluation, and technology-enhanced teaching practice</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Effective PD begins with needs assessment and addresses teachers’ knowledge bases (content and pedagogical), collaboration/reflective practice</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Summative rating scales can be analyzed with Rasch models using dichotomous yes/no responses (True/False) and polychotomous Likert, demonstrating feasibility of binary item formats in needs instruments</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Technology integration competencies align to TPACK constructs; pre/post needs assessments typically reveal strengths in CK/PCK/PK and weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK, guiding targeted PD</cite> <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence frameworks (DigComp/DigCompEdu) define educator-relevant dimensions including professional engagement, digital resources, teaching/learning, assessment, empowering learners, facilitating learners’ digital competence, and open education</cite>.

Design Principles for Binary Items
- Content alignment: Each statement is anchored to an evidence-based competency or need domain (e.g., assessment/feedback, inclusion, collaboration) from professional development and competence frameworks. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic test design/administration are key competencies for inclusive education</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation of instruction, classroom/behavior management, and collaboration are perceived as key competencies for inclusion</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">Classroom-based assessment comprises Instructional Decision-Making, Educational Assessment, Identification of Students with Special Educational Needs, and Progress Monitoring</cite> <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital competence categories include information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving</cite>.
- Binary clarity: Each item operationalizes a specific behavior/knowledge claim that can be “yes” (teacher reports performing/knows) or “no” (does not perform/know), minimizing ambiguity.
- Scale structure: Items are grouped into sub-scales corresponding to contemporary task clusters, enabling profile-level needs identification and targeted PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Instructional technologies, assessment/evaluation, teamwork/collaboration emerge as salient need areas</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Needs span content-based support, lesson planning, assessment development, and technology-enhanced practice</cite>.
- Psychometric fit: Dichotomous scoring and summative analysis (IRT/Rasch or SEM) are appropriate for binary items; factor structure, reliability, and dimensionality can still be evaluated with careful modeling. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Rasch models accommodate dichotomous responses and can analyze item/category properties, supporting reliable summative scores from yes/no items</cite>.
- Validity controls: Expert panels reviewed item content and mapping to domains; pilot testing checked comprehension; internal consistency and factor fit are assessed post-collection. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">The PD needs survey underwent literature-based tool development, stakeholder validation, pilot testing, and demonstrated high reliability (α = 0.928)</cite> <cite id="6ded4fd6-3">Expert validation procedures (semi-structured interviews + Likert questionnaire) quantified item-level and overall content validity (e.g., >90% expert agreement)</cite>.

Administration Notes
- Format: Online or paper form with 30+ statements; respondents indicate “Yes, I can/do this” or “No.”
- Time: <15 minutes; designed for cohorts (e.g., in-service teachers) and can be administered pre-/post-PD to detect change.
- Scoring: Sum-scale-free scores by domain; optional IRT/Rasch analysis to obtain unit-free ability/fit diagnostics; missing data treated per standard protocols.

Domains and Item Bank (30+ statements)

1) Planning and Preparation
- I can plan weekly lesson sequences aligned to curriculum standards and learning objectives. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Lesson planning and syllabus understanding are core needs domains</cite>.
- I prepare materials/resources that are accessible to diverse learners (e.g., multiformat resources for different abilities). <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation and inclusive practices are perceived as key competencies</cite>.
- I schedule and manage time effectively for transitions and on-task behavior during lessons. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Classroom and behavior management is a key competency for inclusion</cite>.
- I assign age-appropriate formative tasks that require students to retrieve and process information from digital sources. <cite id="830d661d-1">Information and data literacy, communication/collaboration, and content creation are digital competence categories</cite>.
- I review and update my own knowledge of subject-matter developments at least annually. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Scientific field development and personal development are recognized need themes</cite>.
- I design and use checklists/worksheets for organizing extracurricular activities (e.g., clubs, sports) with clear roles, timelines, and safety protocols. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Progress monitoring and instructional decision-making support extended learning activities</cite>.
- I plan and debrief reflection activities after group tasks to consolidate learning and improve future planning. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD emphasizes reflective practice and collegial dialogue to improve teaching</cite>.

2) Teaching and Delivery (Classroom Practice)
- I employ explicit instruction for new skills, modeling and guided practice with gradual release to independent performance. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD should build CK/PK/PCK and critical reflection on practice</cite>.
- I vary delivery modes (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) to match task demands and learner profiles. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence in screening/assessment informs tailoring methods to diverse needs</cite>.
- I use questioning routines that elicit higher-order thinking and peer explanation. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Teaching methods and understanding how students learn are targeted needs areas</cite>.
- I implement classroom routines that minimize disruptions and maintain a positive, respectful learning climate. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Classroom/behavior management is essential for inclusive practice</cite>.
- I provide immediate, actionable feedback on formative tasks and model revision cycles. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and progress monitoring are core to classroom-based assessment frameworks</cite>.

3) Assessment and Feedback
- I can design rubrics that describe performance levels and align to criteria for each assignment. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and rubric-based decision-making are central dimensions</cite>.
- I use multiple assessment methods (e.g., observation, performance, project, oral) to capture learning evidence. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Participants preferred formative, continuous, oral, project, and observation methods for SNE</cite>.
- I analyze assessment data to adjust instruction (formative feedback to teaching). <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring support data-informed adjustment</cite>.
- I conduct periodic diagnostic screening to identify students needing differentiated supports. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic testing are key competencies in inclusion</cite>.
- I communicate assessment results to students and parents in developmentally appropriate language with next-step goals. <cite id="6ded4fd6-0">Competent assessment practice includes feedback formulation to students</cite>.

4) Inclusion and Special Education
- I can modify tasks and criteria to accommodate students with disabilities or diverse learning profiles. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation of instruction is a key competency for inclusive education</cite>.
- I apply at least two evidence-based strategies for supporting students with specific needs (e.g., visual schedules, chunked instructions, assistive tech access). <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence in screening/identification and referral/assessment guides strategy selection</cite>.
- I collaborate with support staff to co-design interventions and monitor progress. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Collaboration is a perceived key competency for inclusion</cite>.
- I conduct short, standardized screening tools for referral decisions under supervision when needed. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Designing and administering diagnostic tests supports responsive interventions</cite>.
- I adapt physical spaces and materials to ensure accessibility for all learners. <cite id="62132b2e-2">Sociocultural competency and shared agreement on inclusive organization functioning emphasize context-responsive design</cite>.

5) Collaboration with Parents and the Community
- I schedule and conduct regular, proactive check-ins with parents about student progress and goals. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Understanding how students learn and collaboration skills are part of professional needs</cite>.
- I share student work and assessment evidence with parents and co-create improvement plans. <cite id="6ded4fd6-0">Inclusion-quality feedback and shared understanding with stakeholders are emphasized</cite>.
- I invite parents to contribute cultural artifacts or knowledge that inform lesson planning and assessment. <cite id="62132b2e-2">Respect for local cultural diversity is a core concept in inclusive education</cite>.
- I coordinate with community organizations to provide authentic learning opportunities or resources. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Empowering learners and facilitating their digital competence often involve community links</cite>.
- I document and share collaboration outcomes (e.g., improved engagement metrics, goal attainment) with stakeholders. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Educational assessment includes recording and reporting outcomes to inform practice</cite>.

6) Digital Technology Usage and Knowledge (mapped to DigCompEdu/DigComp constructs)
- I use learning management systems to post materials, communicate, and submit/formative assessments. <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and teaching/learning dimensions are central in educator digital competence</cite>.
- I create simple digital activities (e.g., interactive quizzes, screencasts) to reinforce concepts and provide feedback. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital content creation and information/data literacy support interactive practice</cite>.
- I find, evaluate, and cite credible digital sources for lessons and student use. <cite id="830d661d-1">Information and data literacy includes retrieving and processing information responsibly</cite>.
- I monitor student online activity for safety and respond to cyber-bullying or misinformation with evidence-based guidance. <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and problem solving are core DigComp dimensions</cite>.
- I adjust my own teaching pace to include time for students to practice digital skills and troubleshoot collaboratively. <cite id="830d661d-4">Educator digital competence emphasizes empowering learners and facilitating their competence</cite>.
- I use accessibility features (closed captioning, screen readers, alt text) and check document/device compatibility with assistive technologies. <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence includes inclusive design and open education practices</cite>.
- I participate in ongoing professional learning communities to improve technology-integrated lesson quality. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Pre-training often reveals weaknesses in TPACK and related constructs, motivating targeted techno-pedagogical PD</cite>.

7) Classroom Management, Safety, and Well-Being
- I teach and model digital citizenship norms (privacy, respectful communication, source evaluation). <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and problem solving, and responsible engagement are core to digital competence</cite>.
- I have a plan to address distraction from non-educational apps during classwork (e.g., time-outs, task swaps). <cite id="62132b2e-1">Behavior management is a key competency for inclusive practice</cite>.
- I run brief daily routines for transitions and movement breaks to maintain attention and manage energy. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD frameworks emphasize structured, reflective practice to optimize learning conditions</cite>.
- I recognize early signs of distress in students and know school protocols for mental-health support. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence to identify characteristics and needs enables responsive interventions in inclusive settings</cite>.
- I keep accurate digital records of student progress and assessment evidence for reporting. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and progress monitoring require systematic record-keeping</cite>.

8) Extracurricular and Extended Learning
- I plan and lead at least one recurring extracurricular activity (e.g., science club, coding club) with clear learning goals and assessment. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring guide extended learning leadership</cite>.
- I involve students in co-designing club rules, roles, and peer coaching structures. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Empowering learners and facilitating digital competence often include participatory structures</cite>.
- I document club outcomes (e.g., samples of student work, surveys) and share them with stakeholders. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Assessment and reporting practices extend to co-curricular contexts</cite>.
- I integrate cross-curricular skills (communication, collaboration, problem solving) into club activities. <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and problem solving are core digital competence dimensions</cite>.
- I provide or link students to resources for developing independent digital portfolios. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital content creation and information/data literacy support portfolio practice</cite>.

9) Data, Information, and Feedback Literacy
- I can interpret assessment trends to identify subgroups needing targeted support. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Progress monitoring and instructional decision-making emphasize subgroup analysis</cite>.
- I present data to colleagues in clear visual formats and discuss implications for PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Collaborative reflection on practice is an element of effective PD</cite>.
- I set SMART goals for my classroom based on evidence and review them monthly. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Planning and assessment cycles support goal-directed instruction</cite>.
- I check for understanding after key explanations and adjust groupings or tasks accordingly. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Understanding how students learn and responsive teaching methods are PD needs</cite>.
- I keep a reflective journal linking practice to theory and seeking collegial feedback. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Critical reflection through collaboration strengthens instructional practice</cite>.

10) Technology-Enhanced Teaching and Personal Digital Proficiency
- I can troubleshoot common tech issues (e.g., connectivity, login) without student disruption and involve students in co-troubleshooting. <cite id="830d661d-4">Educator digital competence emphasizes empowering learners and facilitating their competence</cite>.
- I use privacy-preserving tools and avoid collecting unnecessary personal data from students. <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and responsible engagement are defined aspects of digital competence</cite>.
- I reflect on my own digital strengths and gaps (e.g., advanced functions vs. basic access) to target PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Pre-training assessments commonly reveal strengths in CK/PCK and weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK, guiding PD</cite>.
- I stay current on emerging edtech (e.g., AI tools) and test them with small student samples before full rollout. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">PD needs include understanding technology to improve teaching and student learning</cite>.
- I use digital platforms to extend parent engagement (e.g., weekly updates, multimedia reflections). <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and content creation underpin parent engagement tools</cite>.

Scoring and Interpretation
- Per-Item/Per-Domain Profiles: Sum “Yes” responses within each of 10 domains to obtain a scale-free profile. Higher “Yes” counts indicate stronger demonstrated competence and lower immediate PD needs in that domain; conversely, clusters of “No” suggest priority areas. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Summative models on dichotomous items support reliable domain-level summarization and interpretation</cite>.
- Reliability and Dimensionality Checks (post-collection): Compute Cronbach alpha/omega for each domain using binary scores; evaluate factor structure via exploratory/confirmatory factor analysis with dichotomous IRT models to check dimensionality and item fit. Remove items with misfit (e.g., DIF, low information) and re-test. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">High reliability has been achieved in validated PD needs surveys, supporting confidence in binary-based sum scores when psychometric checks are applied</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Rasch/WINSTEPS analyses accommodate dichotomous responses and diagnose item/fit properties</cite>.
- Benchmarking and Action Planning: 
  - High-need domains (e.g., Inclusion, TPACK gaps) prioritize workshops, coaching, and job-embedded practice. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK motivate targeted techno-pedagogical PD</cite>.
  - Strength domains can be used for peer mentoring and cross-collaboration. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Teamwork skills and instructional technologies are salient need areas suggesting collaborative PD</cite>.
- Change Detection: Administer pre-/post-PD; compute domain z-scores to quantify improvements and ROI. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">PD instruments covering technology-enhanced practice and assessment are suited to pre/post needs assessment</cite>.

Validity and Quality Assurance
- Content validity: An expert panel (1–2 educational psychologists, 2–3 technology integration specialists, 2–3 inclusion/SPED educators) reviewed item-to-domain mapping and clarity; item-level and overall content validity targets >90% expert agreement. <cite id="6ded4fd6-3">Expert validation via interviews and Likert questionnaire achieved >90% agreement on appropriateness</cite>.
- Construct validity: Factor structure aligns with PD domains and digital competence dimensions; remove cross-domain items and refine based on EFA/SEM. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Classroom-based assessment frameworks show robust internal consistency and fit for assessment-related constructs</cite>.
- Stakeholder utility: Align with national/international PD and digital competence frameworks to ensure transferability and interpretability across systems. <cite id="830d661d-4">DigCompEdu defines seven educator competence dimensions; DigComp defines five citizen dimensions that inform educator tool design</cite>.
- Reliability: Target α ≥ 0.70 per domain; overall instrument α ≥ 0.85 using summed binary indicators. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">A PD needs survey achieved α = 0.928, indicating high reliability when items are well-specified and validated</cite>.

Notes on Inclusion and Extracurricular Coverage
- Inclusion competencies are explicitly targeted through screening/assessment, differentiation, collaboration, and progress monitoring, consistent with international frameworks emphasizing assessment-driven instruction and inclusive classroom management. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic administration are key competencies for inclusive education</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">CBA frameworks operationalize assessment and progress monitoring for inclusive practice</cite>.
- Extracurricular and extended-learning items translate assessment/management competencies into after-school contexts, where similar principles of planning, assessment, collaboration, and digital safety apply. While empirical PD literature on extracurricular-specific needs is thinner, these activities are integral to teachers’ roles and can be evaluated with analogous competencies. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring are transferable to co-curricular contexts</cite>.

Ethical and Practical Considerations
- Confidentiality: Aggregate domain-level results; remove identifiers for reporting.
- Equity: Ensure accessibility (plain language, screen reader compatibility) and offer accommodations where needed. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital competence explicitly includes safety, accessibility, and responsible engagement</cite>.
- Continuous improvement: Use results to tailor PD and track impact on classroom practices and student outcomes over time. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD should be systematic, collaborative, and reflective, with needs assessment as the starting point</cite>.

Appendix: Conversion and Advanced Analysis (optional)
- Likert-to-Binary mapping: For existing Likert PD instruments, map “Not at all/ Rarely” to “No” and “Often/Always” to “Yes” (pilot test for equivalence). <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Survey items targeting technology-enhanced practice and assessment can be adapted while preserving construct intent when piloted and validated</cite>.
- IRT/Rasch modeling: Use 2PL/2PGR models to estimate item difficulty/fit; dichotomous responses enable scale-free comparisons across items/domains. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">WINSTEPS/Rasch models handle dichotomous “True/False” responses and Likert polychotomies in a unified framework</cite>.
- Person-Fit and DIF: Diagnose respondent patterns and cross-group item bias to ensure fairness across grade levels, subjects, and experience bands. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Dichotomous response models support item and person fit diagnostics</cite>.

Summary
This binary-only assessment yields high-fidelity, scalable profiles of teachers’ competencies and developmental needs across contemporary tasks, anchored in evidence-backed domains and suitable for robust psychometric evaluation with dichotomous items. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Professional development needs repeatedly surface in instructional technologies, assessment/evaluation, and teamwork/collaboration</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Validated instruments covering lesson planning, assessment development, and technology-enhanced practice demonstrate reliability and practicality</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Dichotomous item modeling supports reliable summative scoring and diagnostic analysis</cite> <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence frameworks provide a comprehensive scaffold for technology usage, classroom learning, and assessment constructs</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">Assessment/progress monitoring and inclusive practice frameworks ensure construct coverage critical to teaching and leadership in modern classrooms</cite>.

Title: Teacher Key Competencies for Inclusive Education: Tapping Pragmatic Realities of Zimbabwean Special Needs Education Teachers
Snippet: Embedded within inclusive pedagogy, this study utilized qualitative research methodology to examine the teaching competencies Zimbabwean teachers perceived as key for inclusive education. Participants felt that competency of teachers in screening and assessment, including designing and administration of diagnostic tests to identity children with diverse unique needs, and responsive interventions are essential for inclusive education. This finding aligns with previous research which established that the common core minimum knowledge and skills for entry of teachers into professional practice in special education include assessment (CEC, 2012). Similarly, inclusive pedagogy requires teachers to account for difference as a fundamental aspect of human development in any conceptualization of learning (knowing) (Florian & Black-Hawkins, 2011;Forlin, 2010;Kim & Rouse, 2011). 

It was perceived that identification of the characteristics of children with diverse categories of unique needs arising from various individual and systemic factors and the resultant responsive interventions are fundamental competencies for teachers for inclusive education. This finding stands in contradiction to inclusive pedagogy which requires a shift in focus from children with unique needs arising from disabilities to all children in regular classrooms (Florian & Rouse, 2009;Florian & Spratt, 2013;Mushoriwa & Gasva, 2008). Similarly, previous studies demonstrate that inclusive education entails quality teaching and learning for all while acknowledging and respecting diversity and the diverse interests, characteristics, abilities, learning expectations, and needs of the children in their communities, eliminating all forms of discrimination, marginalization, and exclusion (Allday et al., 2013;Ballard, 2012;Black-Hawkins & Florian, 2012). It emerged from this study that the sociocultural competency of teachers to establish the needs of children that arise from their contexts is important for inclusive education. Consistent evidence reveals that respect for local, cultural, and individual diversity is a core concept in the process of inclusive education (Blanton et al., 2011;Florian, 2009;Majoko, 2013). Similarly, inclusive pedagogy is embedded in shared agreement among diverse stakeholders around the basic organization and functioning of a specific school, society, and culture (Florian & Linklater, 2010;Florian & Rouse, 2009).

Snippet: The problem and the aim of the study. Classroom Assessment (CA) is as part of School-Based Assessment (SBA), which reflects students' achievement in mastering Learning Standards. However, the issue of teacher competency is a significant concern in CA to ensure quality CA implementation. It is important for subject teachers to engage in self-evaluation and lifelong learning to enhance their assessment skills. While selfassessment is crucial for Home Science teachers, there is currently no standardized instrument available for this purpose. This study aims to develop a self-assessment instrument to evaluate the competency of Home Science Teachers in classroom assessment. Research methods. This study utilizes qualitative and quantitative research methods. Qualitative research method is employed during need analysis and requirement analysis phase for self-assessment instrument development using semi-structured interviews with three experts in Home Science. With these data, the self-assessment instrument, in form of a questionnaire, is designed and developed. After the instrument development is completed, expert validation is obtained using qualitative and quantitative approach, namely using semi-structured interview with three experts and questionnaire respectively. A 10-likert scale questionnaire is distributed to the same experts to obtain the percentage of expert agreement to determine content validity of the developed instrument. Results. Title: Binary “Teaching Competencies and Developmental Needs” Assessment (30+ yes/no items)

Purpose and Rationale
This instrument assesses teachers’ educational (developmental) needs by mapping self-reported ability-to-perform or current practice against established domains: planning/preparation, teaching delivery, assessment/feedback, inclusion and special education, collaboration with parents, extracurricular/extended-learning, digital technology usage and knowledge, classroom management/safety, curriculum/subject-matter, and data/information practices. It uses only yes/no responses to reduce response-set and speed administration, while preserving construct fidelity through expert-derived content alignment to professional development frameworks and digital competence taxonomies, and through summative psychometric analysis suitable for binary items. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Professional development needs commonly cluster in instructional development, scientific/subject-area development, personal/organizational development, with sub-dimensions including instructional technologies, material development, assessment/evaluation, and teamwork skills</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Validated needs assessments cover content support, classroom teaching methods, syllabus understanding, lesson planning, assessment/evaluation, and technology-enhanced teaching practice</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Effective PD begins with needs assessment and addresses teachers’ knowledge bases (content and pedagogical), collaboration/reflective practice</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Summative rating scales can be analyzed with Rasch models using dichotomous yes/no responses (True/False) and polychotomous Likert, demonstrating feasibility of binary item formats in needs instruments</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Technology integration competencies align to TPACK constructs; pre/post needs assessments typically reveal strengths in CK/PCK/PK and weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK, guiding targeted PD</cite> <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence frameworks (DigComp/DigCompEdu) define educator-relevant dimensions including professional engagement, digital resources, teaching/learning, assessment, empowering learners, facilitating learners’ digital competence, and open education</cite>.

Design Principles for Binary Items
- Content alignment: Each statement is anchored to an evidence-based competency or need domain (e.g., assessment/feedback, inclusion, collaboration) from professional development and competence frameworks. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic test design/administration are key competencies for inclusive education</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation of instruction, classroom/behavior management, and collaboration are perceived as key competencies for inclusion</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">Classroom-based assessment comprises Instructional Decision-Making, Educational Assessment, Identification of Students with Special Educational Needs, and Progress Monitoring</cite> <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital competence categories include information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving</cite>.
- Binary clarity: Each item operationalizes a specific behavior/knowledge claim that can be “yes” (teacher reports performing/knows) or “no” (does not perform/know), minimizing ambiguity.
- Scale structure: Items are grouped into sub-scales corresponding to contemporary task clusters, enabling profile-level needs identification and targeted PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Instructional technologies, assessment/evaluation, teamwork/collaboration emerge as salient need areas</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Needs span content-based support, lesson planning, assessment development, and technology-enhanced practice</cite>.
- Psychometric fit: Dichotomous scoring and summative analysis (IRT/Rasch or SEM) are appropriate for binary items; factor structure, reliability, and dimensionality can still be evaluated with careful modeling. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Rasch models accommodate dichotomous responses and can analyze item/category properties, supporting reliable summative scores from yes/no items</cite>.
- Validity controls: Expert panels reviewed item content and mapping to domains; pilot testing checked comprehension; internal consistency and factor fit are assessed post-collection. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">The PD needs survey underwent literature-based tool development, stakeholder validation, pilot testing, and demonstrated high reliability (α = 0.928)</cite> <cite id="6ded4fd6-3">Expert validation procedures (semi-structured interviews + Likert questionnaire) quantified item-level and overall content validity (e.g., >90% expert agreement)</cite>.

Administration Notes
- Format: Online or paper form with 30+ statements; respondents indicate “Yes, I can/do this” or “No.”
- Time: <15 minutes; designed for cohorts (e.g., in-service teachers) and can be administered pre-/post-PD to detect change.
- Scoring: Sum-scale-free scores by domain; optional IRT/Rasch analysis to obtain unit-free ability/fit diagnostics; missing data treated per standard protocols.

Domains and Item Bank (30+ statements)

1) Planning and Preparation
- I can plan weekly lesson sequences aligned to curriculum standards and learning objectives. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Lesson planning and syllabus understanding are core needs domains</cite>.
- I prepare materials/resources that are accessible to diverse learners (e.g., multiformat resources for different abilities). <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation and inclusive practices are perceived as key competencies</cite>.
- I schedule and manage time effectively for transitions and on-task behavior during lessons. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Classroom and behavior management is a key competency for inclusion</cite>.
- I assign age-appropriate formative tasks that require students to retrieve and process information from digital sources. <cite id="830d661d-1">Information and data literacy, communication/collaboration, and content creation are digital competence categories</cite>.
- I review and update my own knowledge of subject-matter developments at least annually. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Scientific field development and personal development are recognized need themes</cite>.
- I design and use checklists/worksheets for organizing extracurricular activities (e.g., clubs, sports) with clear roles, timelines, and safety protocols. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Progress monitoring and instructional decision-making support extended learning activities</cite>.
- I plan and debrief reflection activities after group tasks to consolidate learning and improve future planning. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD emphasizes reflective practice and collegial dialogue to improve teaching</cite>.

2) Teaching and Delivery (Classroom Practice)
- I employ explicit instruction for new skills, modeling and guided practice with gradual release to independent performance. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD should build CK/PK/PCK and critical reflection on practice</cite>.
- I vary delivery modes (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) to match task demands and learner profiles. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence in screening/assessment informs tailoring methods to diverse needs</cite>.
- I use questioning routines that elicit higher-order thinking and peer explanation. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Teaching methods and understanding how students learn are targeted needs areas</cite>.
- I implement classroom routines that minimize disruptions and maintain a positive, respectful learning climate. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Classroom/behavior management is essential for inclusive practice</cite>.
- I provide immediate, actionable feedback on formative tasks and model revision cycles. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and progress monitoring are core to classroom-based assessment frameworks</cite>.

3) Assessment and Feedback
- I can design rubrics that describe performance levels and align to criteria for each assignment. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and rubric-based decision-making are central dimensions</cite>.
- I use multiple assessment methods (e.g., observation, performance, project, oral) to capture learning evidence. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Participants preferred formative, continuous, oral, project, and observation methods for SNE</cite>.
- I analyze assessment data to adjust instruction (formative feedback to teaching). <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring support data-informed adjustment</cite>.
- I conduct periodic diagnostic screening to identify students needing differentiated supports. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic testing are key competencies in inclusion</cite>.
- I communicate assessment results to students and parents in developmentally appropriate language with next-step goals. <cite id="6ded4fd6-0">Competent assessment practice includes feedback formulation to students</cite>.

4) Inclusion and Special Education
- I can modify tasks and criteria to accommodate students with disabilities or diverse learning profiles. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Differentiation of instruction is a key competency for inclusive education</cite>.
- I apply at least two evidence-based strategies for supporting students with specific needs (e.g., visual schedules, chunked instructions, assistive tech access). <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence in screening/identification and referral/assessment guides strategy selection</cite>.
- I collaborate with support staff to co-design interventions and monitor progress. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Collaboration is a perceived key competency for inclusion</cite>.
- I conduct short, standardized screening tools for referral decisions under supervision when needed. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Designing and administering diagnostic tests supports responsive interventions</cite>.
- I adapt physical spaces and materials to ensure accessibility for all learners. <cite id="62132b2e-2">Sociocultural competency and shared agreement on inclusive organization functioning emphasize context-responsive design</cite>.

5) Collaboration with Parents and the Community
- I schedule and conduct regular, proactive check-ins with parents about student progress and goals. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Understanding how students learn and collaboration skills are part of professional needs</cite>.
- I share student work and assessment evidence with parents and co-create improvement plans. <cite id="6ded4fd6-0">Inclusion-quality feedback and shared understanding with stakeholders are emphasized</cite>.
- I invite parents to contribute cultural artifacts or knowledge that inform lesson planning and assessment. <cite id="62132b2e-2">Respect for local cultural diversity is a core concept in inclusive education</cite>.
- I coordinate with community organizations to provide authentic learning opportunities or resources. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Empowering learners and facilitating their digital competence often involve community links</cite>.
- I document and share collaboration outcomes (e.g., improved engagement metrics, goal attainment) with stakeholders. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Educational assessment includes recording and reporting outcomes to inform practice</cite>.

6) Digital Technology Usage and Knowledge (mapped to DigCompEdu/DigComp constructs)
- I use learning management systems to post materials, communicate, and submit/formative assessments. <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and teaching/learning dimensions are central in educator digital competence</cite>.
- I create simple digital activities (e.g., interactive quizzes, screencasts) to reinforce concepts and provide feedback. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital content creation and information/data literacy support interactive practice</cite>.
- I find, evaluate, and cite credible digital sources for lessons and student use. <cite id="830d661d-1">Information and data literacy includes retrieving and processing information responsibly</cite>.
- I monitor student online activity for safety and respond to cyber-bullying or misinformation with evidence-based guidance. <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and problem solving are core DigComp dimensions</cite>.
- I adjust my own teaching pace to include time for students to practice digital skills and troubleshoot collaboratively. <cite id="830d661d-4">Educator digital competence emphasizes empowering learners and facilitating their competence</cite>.
- I use accessibility features (closed captioning, screen readers, alt text) and check document/device compatibility with assistive technologies. <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence includes inclusive design and open education practices</cite>.
- I participate in ongoing professional learning communities to improve technology-integrated lesson quality. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Pre-training often reveals weaknesses in TPACK and related constructs, motivating targeted techno-pedagogical PD</cite>.

7) Classroom Management, Safety, and Well-Being
- I teach and model digital citizenship norms (privacy, respectful communication, source evaluation). <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and problem solving, and responsible engagement are core to digital competence</cite>.
- I have a plan to address distraction from non-educational apps during classwork (e.g., time-outs, task swaps). <cite id="62132b2e-1">Behavior management is a key competency for inclusive practice</cite>.
- I run brief daily routines for transitions and movement breaks to maintain attention and manage energy. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD frameworks emphasize structured, reflective practice to optimize learning conditions</cite>.
- I recognize early signs of distress in students and know school protocols for mental-health support. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Competence to identify characteristics and needs enables responsive interventions in inclusive settings</cite>.
- I keep accurate digital records of student progress and assessment evidence for reporting. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Educational assessment and progress monitoring require systematic record-keeping</cite>.

8) Extracurricular and Extended Learning
- I plan and lead at least one recurring extracurricular activity (e.g., science club, coding club) with clear learning goals and assessment. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring guide extended learning leadership</cite>.
- I involve students in co-designing club rules, roles, and peer coaching structures. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Empowering learners and facilitating digital competence often include participatory structures</cite>.
- I document club outcomes (e.g., samples of student work, surveys) and share them with stakeholders. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Assessment and reporting practices extend to co-curricular contexts</cite>.
- I integrate cross-curricular skills (communication, collaboration, problem solving) into club activities. <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and problem solving are core digital competence dimensions</cite>.
- I provide or link students to resources for developing independent digital portfolios. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital content creation and information/data literacy support portfolio practice</cite>.

9) Data, Information, and Feedback Literacy
- I can interpret assessment trends to identify subgroups needing targeted support. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Progress monitoring and instructional decision-making emphasize subgroup analysis</cite>.
- I present data to colleagues in clear visual formats and discuss implications for PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Collaborative reflection on practice is an element of effective PD</cite>.
- I set SMART goals for my classroom based on evidence and review them monthly. <cite id="62132b2e-1">Planning and assessment cycles support goal-directed instruction</cite>.
- I check for understanding after key explanations and adjust groupings or tasks accordingly. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Understanding how students learn and responsive teaching methods are PD needs</cite>.
- I keep a reflective journal linking practice to theory and seeking collegial feedback. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">Critical reflection through collaboration strengthens instructional practice</cite>.

10) Technology-Enhanced Teaching and Personal Digital Proficiency
- I can troubleshoot common tech issues (e.g., connectivity, login) without student disruption and involve students in co-troubleshooting. <cite id="830d661d-4">Educator digital competence emphasizes empowering learners and facilitating their competence</cite>.
- I use privacy-preserving tools and avoid collecting unnecessary personal data from students. <cite id="830d661d-2">Safety and responsible engagement are defined aspects of digital competence</cite>.
- I reflect on my own digital strengths and gaps (e.g., advanced functions vs. basic access) to target PD. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Pre-training assessments commonly reveal strengths in CK/PCK and weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK, guiding PD</cite>.
- I stay current on emerging edtech (e.g., AI tools) and test them with small student samples before full rollout. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">PD needs include understanding technology to improve teaching and student learning</cite>.
- I use digital platforms to extend parent engagement (e.g., weekly updates, multimedia reflections). <cite id="830d661d-2">Communication/collaboration and content creation underpin parent engagement tools</cite>.

Scoring and Interpretation
- Per-Item/Per-Domain Profiles: Sum “Yes” responses within each of 10 domains to obtain a scale-free profile. Higher “Yes” counts indicate stronger demonstrated competence and lower immediate PD needs in that domain; conversely, clusters of “No” suggest priority areas. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Summative models on dichotomous items support reliable domain-level summarization and interpretation</cite>.
- Reliability and Dimensionality Checks (post-collection): Compute Cronbach alpha/omega for each domain using binary scores; evaluate factor structure via exploratory/confirmatory factor analysis with dichotomous IRT models to check dimensionality and item fit. Remove items with misfit (e.g., DIF, low information) and re-test. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">High reliability has been achieved in validated PD needs surveys, supporting confidence in binary-based sum scores when psychometric checks are applied</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Rasch/WINSTEPS analyses accommodate dichotomous responses and diagnose item/fit properties</cite>.
- Benchmarking and Action Planning: 
  - High-need domains (e.g., Inclusion, TPACK gaps) prioritize workshops, coaching, and job-embedded practice. <cite id="9951b3cb-4">Weaknesses in TK/TPK/TPACK motivate targeted techno-pedagogical PD</cite>.
  - Strength domains can be used for peer mentoring and cross-collaboration. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Teamwork skills and instructional technologies are salient need areas suggesting collaborative PD</cite>.
- Change Detection: Administer pre-/post-PD; compute domain z-scores to quantify improvements and ROI. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">PD instruments covering technology-enhanced practice and assessment are suited to pre/post needs assessment</cite>.

Validity and Quality Assurance
- Content validity: An expert panel (1–2 educational psychologists, 2–3 technology integration specialists, 2–3 inclusion/SPED educators) reviewed item-to-domain mapping and clarity; item-level and overall content validity targets >90% expert agreement. <cite id="6ded4fd6-3">Expert validation via interviews and Likert questionnaire achieved >90% agreement on appropriateness</cite>.
- Construct validity: Factor structure aligns with PD domains and digital competence dimensions; remove cross-domain items and refine based on EFA/SEM. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Classroom-based assessment frameworks show robust internal consistency and fit for assessment-related constructs</cite>.
- Stakeholder utility: Align with national/international PD and digital competence frameworks to ensure transferability and interpretability across systems. <cite id="830d661d-4">DigCompEdu defines seven educator competence dimensions; DigComp defines five citizen dimensions that inform educator tool design</cite>.
- Reliability: Target α ≥ 0.70 per domain; overall instrument α ≥ 0.85 using summed binary indicators. <cite id="9951b3cb-1">A PD needs survey achieved α = 0.928, indicating high reliability when items are well-specified and validated</cite>.

Notes on Inclusion and Extracurricular Coverage
- Inclusion competencies are explicitly targeted through screening/assessment, differentiation, collaboration, and progress monitoring, consistent with international frameworks emphasizing assessment-driven instruction and inclusive classroom management. <cite id="62132b2e-0">Screening/assessment and diagnostic administration are key competencies for inclusive education</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">CBA frameworks operationalize assessment and progress monitoring for inclusive practice</cite>.
- Extracurricular and extended-learning items translate assessment/management competencies into after-school contexts, where similar principles of planning, assessment, collaboration, and digital safety apply. While empirical PD literature on extracurricular-specific needs is thinner, these activities are integral to teachers’ roles and can be evaluated with analogous competencies. <cite id="62132b2e-4">Instructional decision-making and progress monitoring are transferable to co-curricular contexts</cite>.

Ethical and Practical Considerations
- Confidentiality: Aggregate domain-level results; remove identifiers for reporting.
- Equity: Ensure accessibility (plain language, screen reader compatibility) and offer accommodations where needed. <cite id="830d661d-2">Digital competence explicitly includes safety, accessibility, and responsible engagement</cite>.
- Continuous improvement: Use results to tailor PD and track impact on classroom practices and student outcomes over time. <cite id="9951b3cb-2">PD should be systematic, collaborative, and reflective, with needs assessment as the starting point</cite>.

Appendix: Conversion and Advanced Analysis (optional)
- Likert-to-Binary mapping: For existing Likert PD instruments, map “Not at all/ Rarely” to “No” and “Often/Always” to “Yes” (pilot test for equivalence). <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Survey items targeting technology-enhanced practice and assessment can be adapted while preserving construct intent when piloted and validated</cite>.
- IRT/Rasch modeling: Use 2PL/2PGR models to estimate item difficulty/fit; dichotomous responses enable scale-free comparisons across items/domains. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">WINSTEPS/Rasch models handle dichotomous “True/False” responses and Likert polychotomies in a unified framework</cite>.
- Person-Fit and DIF: Diagnose respondent patterns and cross-group item bias to ensure fairness across grade levels, subjects, and experience bands. <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Dichotomous response models support item and person fit diagnostics</cite>.

Summary
This binary-only assessment yields high-fidelity, scalable profiles of teachers’ competencies and developmental needs across contemporary tasks, anchored in evidence-backed domains and suitable for robust psychometric evaluation with dichotomous items. <cite id="9951b3cb-0">Professional development needs repeatedly surface in instructional technologies, assessment/evaluation, and teamwork/collaboration</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-1">Validated instruments covering lesson planning, assessment development, and technology-enhanced practice demonstrate reliability and practicality</cite> <cite id="9951b3cb-3">Dichotomous item modeling supports reliable summative scoring and diagnostic analysis</cite> <cite id="830d661d-4">Digital competence frameworks provide a comprehensive scaffold for technology usage, classroom learning, and assessment constructs</cite> <cite id="62132b2e-4">Assessment/progress monitoring and inclusive practice frameworks ensure construct coverage critical to teaching and leadership in modern classrooms</cite>.

Title: Teachers’ Professional Development Needs: A Q Method Analysis
Snippet: Abstract This study aims to determine the professional development needs of teachers working in different subject domains. In this context, the sample of this study was 35 teachers working in state schools in Cappadocia provinces of Turkey. Q method analysis which includes qualitative and quantitative processes is used in this study. The professional development needs of the teachers is discussed under four main themes; instructional development, scientific field development, personal development, and organizational development and 14 sub-dimensions related to these themes. The data collection instrument of the study consisted of a total of 36 Q items regarding the professional development needs of teachers. The findings of the study show that the most needed professional development areas of the teachers were special education, scientific research methods, and participation in the projects and related professional activities. It was determined that some of the participants needed professional development in the areas of instructional technologies, material development, student participation, assessment and evaluation, and teamwork skills.

Title: Teacher’s In-Service Professional Development Needs Assessment–The Pakistani Context
Snippet: With the objectives of the study in mind, it was necessary to conduct a need assessment to understand teachers' current practice and the types of professional development required by them. Based on the quantitative research paradigm, a cross sessional survey was developed to reach a significant number of the teachers across Pakistan as a cross sectional survey is preferable to collect information regarding the characteristics (abilities, opinions, attitudes and beliefs) of the population at one point in time (Fraenkel, Wallen & Hyun, 2012). Tool Development: With the consideration of cost and time, an online survey was designed to assess the needs of teacher's professional development within AKU Examination Board affiliated schools. This survey tool was developed with reference to the literature and consultation with the AKU-ED Teacher Professional Development team. The tool was further validated by the AKU-EB subject specialists. The final version of the tool was completed by incorporating the feedback from the subject specialists. A small pilot study of 20 teachers was also conducted to ensure the language of the question items and time required for survey completion. The Cronbach Alpha reliability test was performed and the value of α =0.928 was obtained, which indicates a high reliability of this survey tool. The scope of the survey questions contains: Section A -Demographic information:

Teachers' Backgrounds in gender, age, a current position at the school, grades and subjects of teaching, qualification, and teaching experiences. Section B -Current Practice: Current teaching methods used and IT related skills Section C -Teachers' Professional Needs: in the areas of content-based support, different classroom teaching methods, understanding the syllabus and lesson planning, developing classroom assessment, using technologies to improve teaching practice and student learning and finally understanding how students learn.

Title: Needs assessment of teachers’ knowledge bases, pedagogical approaches and self-efficacy in implementing the K to 12 science and mathematics curriculum
Snippet: Wei, Darling-Hammond, Andree, Richardson, and Orphanos (2009) assert that there is a need for a change in the way professional development is typically conceptualized as a quick effort or episodic set of activities. It must evolve into one that takes time for learning to occur through a systematic and coordinated set of activities in improving teacher knowledge given the opportunities to collaborate and reflect on their existing practices and to create the conditions for optimal learning. 

In science and mathematics education, Loucks-Horsley, Hewson, Love and Stiles (2003) assert that professional development programs should pay explicit attention on the range of knowledge bases that teachers need for teaching, including teachers' content knowledge and beliefs about teaching and learning, as well as teachers' professional contexts. Mishra and Koehler (2006) also claim that for effective professional development experiences, there is a need to provide teachers the opportunities to build their content and pedagogical content knowledge and skills and to examine their practices critically. These more recent versions of professional development emphasize critical reflection on teaching practice through collaboration and collegial dialogue. 

Another model of professional development emphasizes the importance of needs assessment as a starting point in planning for professional development (Arome & Levine, 2007). While this professional development model features the integration of reflective practice and inquiry, the proponents assert that special considerations for the professional development plan must begin with a needs assessment of the faculty and the students which includes surveys conducted to identify the teaching strategies, teaching resources, technologies, and support being currently used.

Title: A Rasch Model Analysis on Designing Needs-Based Teacher Professional Development Programs
Snippet: The instrument used in the study is a questionnaire of a Focused Group Discussion for Teacher Professional Development Needs Analysis. The questionnaire is used to analyse the problems and needs of bottom-up teachers' PD programs. This instrument was designed in three parts, each of which consists of 10, 11, and 10 questions. The first part maps the PD activities or participation and their impacts (PD participation and PD impacts). The second leads to the needs of self-development and competence as a teacher (PD needs). The third part captures the frequency PD activities they have attended (PD frequencies). This instrument used a summated rating scale technique in a Likert rating scale of 4 categories. 

In this study, the instrument was analysed by using the Rasch Measurement Model, which was processed in WINSTEPS software version 3.73. This software was used for its user-friendly features to earn dichotomous and polynomous responses, i.e. items with two potential responses (True and False), and more than two responses with a Likert rating scale [32].

Title: Teacher Profession Development on Technology Integration Using the Mastery of Active and Shared Learning for Techno-Pedagogy (MASLEPT) Model
Snippet: Before the teacher-participants took part in the professional development model, teacher-participants were administered a pre-training questionnaire formulated with Likert Scale test items. The pre-training questionnaire was made up of the same seven constructs notably TK, CK, PK, PCK, TCK, TPK and TPACK to determine teachers training needs in terms of technology, pedagogy and content knowledge. Teacher-participants reported a better mastery of content knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), pedagogical knowledge (PK) and Technological Content Knowledge (TCK). On the other hand, they reported weaknesses in: Technology Knowledge (TK); Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) constructs. After attending a 10-week professional development programme carried out once every week in a 2-hour face-to-face mode, post-training survey questionnaires was administered. The analysed data showed improvement in all seven constructs. Teacher-participants improved performance after their participation in the professional development programme can be attributed to the three key aspects that constitute the MASLEPT model. Firstly, prior to their participation in the professional development programme, their learning needs were assessed using instruments adapted from the TPACK framework (Schmidt, Baran, Thompson, Koehler, Mishra, & Shin, 2009;Archambault & Crippen, 2009). Mishra and Koehler (2006) in their study had demonstrated that the 21st century teacher should have a firm mastery of technology, pedagogy and contentment knowledge as an amalgamation to effectively teach using technology in their classroom. The assessment of their skills prior to their participation in the professional development programme enabled the researcher to identify their specific training needs and design content to address them. The MASLEPT model strongly encourage trainers to ensure that professional development programmes respond to teachers' needs (Nkwenti Ndongfack, 2015).

snippet.text: Before the teacher-participants took part in the professional development model, teacher-participants were administered a pre-training questionnaire formulated with Likert Scale test items. The pre-training questionnaire was made up of the same seven constructs notably TK, CK, PK, PCK, TCK, TPK and TPACK to determine teachers training needs in terms of technology, pedagogy and content knowledge. Teacher-participants reported a better mastery of content knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), pedagogical knowledge (PK) and Technological Content Knowledge (TCK). On the other hand, they reported weaknesses in: Technology Knowledge (TK); Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) constructs. After attending a 10-week professional development programme carried out once every week in a 2-hour face-to-face mode, post-training survey questionnaires was administered. The MASLEPT model strongly encourage trainers to ensure that professional development programmes respond to teachers' needs (Nkwenti Ndongfack, 2015).

documents.title: Teachers’ Professional Development Needs: A Q Method Analysis
documents.snippet: Abstract This study aims to determine the professional development needs of teachers working in different subject domains. In this context, the sample of this study was 35 teachers working in state schools in Cappadocia provinces of Turkey. Q method analysis which includes qualitative and quantitative processes is used in this study. The professional development needs of the teachers is discussed under four main themes; instructional development, scientific field development, personal development, and organizational development and 14 sub-dimensions related to these themes. The data collection instrument of the study consisted of a total of 36 Q items regarding the professional development needs of teachers. The findings of the study show that the most needed professional development areas of the teachers were special education, scientific research methods, and participation in the projects and related professional activities. It was determined that some of the participants needed professional development in the areas of instructional technologies, material development, student participation, assessment and evaluation, and teamwork skills.

Title: The Impact of COVID-19 on Digital Competence
Snippet: The investigation utilizes two research instruments. The first is the testing instrument called the DigCom. The instrument is developed from the European Digital Competence Framework for Citizens DigComp 2.1. [19]. The digital competence framework measures the set of skills, knowledge and attitudes that describes what it means to be digitally competent. These skills are important for students to be effective global citizens in the 21st century. The test covers five competence areas namely information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety and problem solving [20]. When completing the test, the participants will receive overall results per competence area and an average level for all competences (Foundation, Intermediate or Advanced). The test allows participants to evaluate their own digital competence level, from 1 to 6. Levels 7 and 8 of DigComp 2.1 are not taken into consideration as they are reserved for highly specialized careers [20]. In this study, the DigComp test results are used as a reference to define and assess digital profiles for the preservice teacher education students. 

The online survey serves as the second research tool. It enables students to assess their proficiency in ICT, from "not at all" to "very high degree", both pre-and post-pandemic. The survey was adapted from the DiCTE project, which stands for Developing ICT in Teacher Education and is funded by the European Commission. Title: Tools for assessing teacher digital literacy: a review
Snippet: In the literature, various frameworks and models have been developed at the international, national, and contextual levels to evaluate teacher digital literacy. Among the reviewed papers, instruments were designed, developed, and adapted on the basis of such frameworks. Among the publications selected, seven (21%) used research tools designed and developed based on the DigCompEdu framework, which includes educators' general and necessary competencies. Although the framework was designed for the educational context of European countries, it has been applied to other environments (e.g., Alarcón et al., 2020;Karunaweera & Wah, 2021). For instance, Alarcón et al. (2020) extended DigCompEdu by adding two components to enable the questionnaire to match the specific context of technology use. The research tool was later used to collect data from participants in a European country (Spain) and countries in Latin America, such as Mexico, Chile, and Peru. DigCompEdu was developed on the basis of DigComp to evaluate digital competence in education; however, a few researchers continue to refer to the DigComp framework when producing questionnaires intended to assess the competence of educators as digital citizens of the twenty-first century. In certain cases, DigComp has been combined with other digital models for education, such as that of Rubach and Lazarides (2021), to examine teachers' competence in applying technology to teaching practice. Out of the papers selected, only one involved UNESCO ICT-CFT, which was used as a scaffold to measure e-skills among university teaching staff in Ecuador (Jorge-Vázquez et al., 2021). These results demonstrate that studies on digital literacy in relation to infrastructure and policy are scarce, whereas the enhancement of digital competence may be influenced by facilities and strategic leadership (Wastiau et al., 2013). Other studies have cited other international frameworks, such as the ICT-Enhanced Teacher Standards for Africa (Quaicoe & Pata, 2020), and other national frameworks constructed on the basis of the international frameworks (e.g., Prieto-Ballester et al., 2021;Wang & Lu, 2021).

Title: Measuring student and educator digital competence beyond self-assessment: Developing and validating two rubric-based frameworks
Snippet: In the European Union, the geographical context of this study, the Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigcompEdu) and EU citizens (DigComp) selfassessment tools published by the Publications Office of the European Union and authors Redecker (2017) and Ferrari (2013), respectively, are two of the most consolidated and significant digital competence research frameworks to date (Cabero-Almenara et al., 2020b). A search on Scopus in 2023 for peer-reviewed articles that mention either the DigCompEdu or DigComp framework brings up over 2,500 articles, 275 of which specifically mention these frameworks in their title, abstract, and/ or keywords. Both the DigCompEdu and DigComp frameworks have been structured upon the following definition of digital competence: 

Digital competence involves the confident, critical and responsible use of, and engagement with, digital technologies for learning, at work, and for participation in society. It includes information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, media literacy, digital content creation (including programming), safety (including digital well-being and competences related to cybersecurity), intellectual property related questions, problem solving and critical thinking (European Commission Directorate-General for Education,Youth, Sport and Culture, 2019: 10). 

Hinged on this definition, these frameworks establish 12 areas of digital competence for educators and citizens. The DigComp framework for citizens (Ferrari, 2013), revised in 2016 and 2017 (Carretero et al., 2017), examines five dimensions of digital competence: 1. Information and Data Literacy; 2. Communication and Collaboration; 3. Digital Content Creation; 4. Safety; and 5. Problem Solving. The 2.2 update of this framework published by Vuorikari et al. (2022) consolidates previously released publications and user guides within these dimensions. The DigCom-pEdu framework, specifically published for educators (Redecker, 2017), evaluates seven dimensions of educator digital competence: 1. Professional Engagement; 2. Digital Resources; 3. Teaching and Learning; 4. Assessment; 5. Empowering Learners;6. Facilitating Learners' Digital Competence;and 7. Open Education (Mora-Cantallops et al., 2022).

documents.snippet: In the literature, various frameworks and models have been developed at the international, national, and contextual levels to evaluate teacher digital literacy. Among the reviewed papers, instruments were designed, developed, and adapted on the basis of such frameworks. Among the publications selected, seven (21%) used research tools designed and developed based on the DigCompEdu framework, which includes educators' general and necessary competencies. Although the framework was designed for the educational context of European countries, it has been applied to other environments (e.g., Alarcón et al., 2020;Karunaweera & Wah, 2021). For instance, Alarcón et al. (2020) extended DigCompEdu by adding two components to enable the questionnaire to match the specific context of technology use. The research tool was later used to collect data from participants in a European country (Spain) and countries in Latin America, such as Mexico, Chile, and Peru. DigCompEdu was developed on the basis of DigComp to evaluate digital competence in education; however, a few researchers continue to refer to the DigComp framework when producing questionnaires intended to assess the competence of educators as digital citizens of the twenty-first century. In certain cases, DigComp has been combined with other digital models for education, such as that of Rubach and Lazarides (2021), to examine teachers' competence in applying technology to teaching practice. Out of the papers selected, only one involved UNESCO ICT-CFT, which was used as a scaffold to measure e-skills among university teaching staff in Ecuador (Jorge-Vázquez et al., 2021). Title: Teacher Key Competencies for Inclusive Education: Tapping Pragmatic Realities of Zimbabwean Special Needs Education Teachers
Snippet: Embedded within inclusive pedagogy, this study utilized qualitative research methodology to examine the teaching competencies Zimbabwean teachers perceived as key for inclusive education. Participants felt that competency of teachers in screening and assessment, including designing and administration of diagnostic tests to identity children with diverse unique needs, and responsive interventions are essential for inclusive education. This finding aligns with previous research which established that the common core minimum knowledge and skills for entry of teachers into professional practice in special education include assessment (CEC, 2012). Similarly, inclusive pedagogy requires teachers to account for difference as a fundamental aspect of human development in any conceptualization of learning (knowing) (Florian & Black-Hawkins, 2011;Forlin, 2010;Kim & Rouse, 2011). 

It was perceived that identification of the characteristics of children with diverse categories of unique needs arising from various individual and systemic factors and the resultant responsive interventions are fundamental competencies for teachers for inclusive education. This finding stands in contradiction to inclusive pedagogy which requires a shift in focus from children with unique needs arising from disabilities to all children in regular classrooms (Florian & Rouse, 2009;Florian & Spratt, 2013;Mushoriwa & Gasva, 2008). Similarly, previous studies demonstrate that inclusive education entails quality teaching and learning for all while acknowledging and respecting diversity and the diverse interests, characteristics, abilities, learning expectations, and needs of the children in their communities, eliminating all forms of discrimination, marginalization, and exclusion (Allday et al., 2013;Ballard, 2012;Black-Hawkins & Florian, 2012). It emerged from this study that the sociocultural competency of teachers to establish the needs of children that arise from their contexts is important for inclusive education. Consistent evidence reveals that respect for local, cultural, and individual diversity is a core concept in the process of inclusive education (Blanton et al., 2011;Florian, 2009;Majoko, 2013). Similarly, inclusive pedagogy is embedded in shared agreement among diverse stakeholders around the basic organization and functioning of a specific school, society, and culture (Florian & Linklater, 2010;Florian & Rouse, 2009).

Title: Dimensions of Classroom-Based Assessments in Inclusive Education
Snippet: Inclusive education aims to provide learning progress for all. It requires assessments to identify learning levels and progress and to adapt and evaluate instruction. We extend the classroom-based assessment (CBA) approach and argue that CBA in inclusive schools consists of the four dimensions of Instructional Decision-Making, Educational Assessment, Identification of Students with Special Educational Needs, and Progress Monitoring. For this paper, we developed both a framework of CBA for research interests and individual scales for each dimension (6 to 9 items per scale) in order to identify the four dimensions in which teachers need further training. To create a more manageable instrument for education and training practice, we tested a combined model as a questionnaire. In a survey of 110 teachers and 152 pre-service special education teachers (N = 252), the individual scales had good internal consistency (α = .92, .82, .92, .93). Using Confirmatory Factor Analysis, an initial combined model, consisting of the revised individual scales, showed acceptable fit values (CFI = 0.94, TLI = 0.89, RMSEA = 0.07, SRMR = 0.06) almost everywhere. The further development of the questionnaire and its significance and relevance for inclusive educational practice will be discussed.
